nameStory: The Red-bellied Pacu gets its name from the vibrant reddish-orange coloring that develops on the belly and lower body of juvenile fish. As these South American natives grow larger, this striking red coloration often fades, but the name stuck from their eye-catching younger days. The word 'pacu' comes from the Tupi indigenous language of Brazil, where these fish naturally swim in Amazon rivers.
description: The Red-bellied Pacu is a large, deep-bodied freshwater fish that's actually a close cousin of the famous piranha, though it's much more peaceful. These South American natives have a distinctive disc-like, compressed body shape and can grow quite large - sometimes reaching the size of a dinner plate. While they're not native to New England waters, occasional specimens turn up when former aquarium fish are released into local waterways. Unlike their piranha relatives, pacus are primarily plant-eaters with human-like square teeth instead of razor-sharp triangular ones.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Deep, laterally compressed body that's almost disc-like when viewed from the side, feeling solid and muscular to the touch with smooth, slippery scales

idTips.label: Mouth
idTips.description: Square, human-like teeth that feel blunt rather than sharp - completely different from the needle-sharp triangular teeth of piranhas

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Juveniles show bright red-orange coloring on the belly and fins, while adults are more silvery-gray with darker edges on fins and sometimes faint reddish hints

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Can reach impressive sizes much larger than most New England natives, with adults potentially growing to the size of a large dinner plate

idTips.label: Fins
idTips.description: Single dorsal fin positioned high on the back, with all fins feeling thick and fleshy, often showing dark edges or spots

habitat: Red-bellied Pacus are not naturally found in New England waters, but the rare individual might appear in warmer lakes, ponds, or slow-moving rivers during summer months after being released from aquariums. They prefer warm water and would only survive in our region during the warmest months before cold weather kills them. Any pacu found here would likely be near urban areas where aquarium releases are more common.

seasonality.spring: Any pacu in New England waters would be struggling in the still-cool spring temperatures, likely appearing sluggish and staying in the warmest, shallowest areas available.
seasonality.summer: Peak season for potential pacu sightings, when recently-released aquarium fish might temporarily survive in our warmest lakes and ponds before winter temperatures prove fatal.
seasonality.fall: Cooling water temperatures would stress any pacu present, making them increasingly lethargic and vulnerable as they cannot survive New England winters.
seasonality.winter: No pacus would survive New England winter conditions - any present would die from the cold temperatures that drop well below their tropical requirements.

funFact: Pacus have become internet famous for having teeth that look remarkably like human molars - so much so that dentists have used photos of pacu teeth in presentations, and the resemblance is so uncanny it often makes people do a double-take!
confusionNotes: Red-bellied Pacus are most commonly confused with piranhas due to their similar body shape and family relationship, but remember: pacus have square, human-like teeth for crushing plants while piranhas have triangular, razor-sharp teeth for tearing flesh. Think 'square teeth = safe pacu, triangle teeth = dangerous piranha.'
contextualKnowledge: There's widespread confusion about pacu species identification, with multiple different South American fish all being called 'red-bellied pacu' in the aquarium trade. This has led to mixed-up information about their care needs and behavior, contributing to inappropriate releases when aquarium owners can no longer care for these large, long-lived fish.
compareHints: Since no other Piaractus species occur in New England, compare the Red-bellied Pacu to other members of its family like silver dollars, which are much smaller and more compressed. Pacus are significantly larger and more robust than silver dollars, with a deeper body profile and those distinctive human-like teeth that set them apart from all their piranha-family relatives.
